source.title: A Scaling Study for fMRI Foundation Models
source.authors: Wen-Hao Ye; Xuan-Ye Pan; Jun-Feng Xia; Jun-Xiang Zhang; Mo Wang; Quan-Ying Liu

record.tranche_reason: The study tests resource-scaling relationships for fMRI models, a different modality, using downstream linear-probe performance rather than language-model pretraining loss.
record.gate_note: The paper varies fMRI pretraining data, model size, and training progress and reports downstream performance trends and fitted-response results. It explicitly describes the observed grid rather than fitting or extrapolating a universal power law. The language-model loss results cited in related work are not results of this study.
record.test_reason: The study sweeps pretraining data (about 24.5-fold), encoder size (2.65M–92.59M) and training progress for fMRI JEPA models. It reports how frozen linear-probe downstream performance changes with scale (V6). It also fits a Muennighoff-style effective-data power-law response to ID downstream error, with grouped holdouts (V5: other modality and repeated data). It reports no pretraining loss, no allocation exponents, no architecture-shape comparison and no far extrapolation.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely right. The authors conclude that compute alone does not characterise fMRI scaling: downstream performance depends on how data, model size and training duration are combined. Data gains are larger for larger models. At matched compute, more data helps more tasks than a larger model. An ID-fitted response selects fixed-budget models that achieve the best average OOD performance among compared baselines, without a universal allocation rule or far extrapolation.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses fMRI pretraining and downstream linear-probe scores, not language-model held-out cross-entropy or the original language-model scaling-law measurements. It fixes one architecture family and objective, sweeps data, size, and progress, and fits an effective-data downstream response within its observed grid.
record.method_sensitivity: Outcome varies by task and resource allocation; interaction estimates differ across training progress. The authors report that source composition is held fixed, task-resampling uncertainty omits independent pretraining-run variation, and repeated data exposure requires a fitted diminishing-return correction.

fits_no_version.finding: The data-by-model-size interaction in fitted downstream scores is positive at every training stage (0.123 to 0.239) and larger at the endpoint (Δ=0.116, CI [0.006, 0.216]).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Gains from more pretraining data grow with model size (data and model should be scaled together), and this complementarity strengthens with training.

fits_no_version.finding: At matched compute (0.11–2.60 EFLOP), 8 of 12 fMRI tasks favour more data, 4 are unresolved and none favours a larger model. With a 0.20 EFLOP lower bound, the split is 6 data-favoured and 6 unresolved.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In data-constrained modalities, at matched compute, extra data beats extra parameters for downstream performance.

record.code_released: not stated (the paper says code is available at link, but no URL is present in the text)
record.problems: The study uses one fixed method and ROI-time architecture family; the observed data range is approximately 24.5-fold and no substantially larger configuration is reserved for prospective testing. The fitted response is not validated far beyond the observed range. Task resampling omits independent pretraining-run variation, and baseline compute values are estimates.
record.rows_left_out: The public-model OOD table contains many per-model task metrics, but those comparisons do not separately test scale-response trends; the aggregate selected-model outcome is recorded in R23. Details of prior studies cited in the paper are not this study's results.

untested.parts: No held-out pretraining loss is reported or fitted.
No extrapolation to larger runs. The authors say the response cannot predict far beyond the about 24.5-fold data range.
No estimate of compute-optimal N and D as powers of compute. The matched-compute data-versus-model comparisons are grid-descriptive.
No comparison of depth or width at fixed parameter count.
Pretraining-loss power laws in fMRI. Ranges spanning several orders of magnitude. Image, video and fine-tuning regimes.
Language-model downstream tasks, and downstream performance as a function of pretraining loss.
No comparison of exponents or compute-optimal split across fitting choices or published laws. The only sensitivity check (raw vs smoothed, weighted vs unweighted) reports similar estimates.

missing.what: Sensitivity of the matched-compute contrast to the averaging range (lower bound 0.20 EFLOP: 6 tasks data-favoured, 6 unresolved)
OOD audit: the ID-selected models rank 8/35 and 24/42 among eligible candidates (regret 0.0211, 0.0359), so the ID fit does not pick the OOD-best configuration
missing.versions: V6 (transfer of fitted predictability across task groups)

missing.what: Robustness of the fit: raw vs smoothed trajectories and run-balanced vs unweighted objectives give similar RMSE and data-decay estimates

record.verdict_notes: The reader's V7 links were moved to V5: the formulation comparisons test whether the repeated-data power-law form fits a new modality. They are not tests of fit-dependence across published laws. R21–R22 are in-sample selection values and R23 is a method comparison. The interaction and matched-compute rows do not estimate V3 allocation exponents. Measures throughout are downstream probe scores, not pretraining loss. Ranges are about 24.5-fold in data and about 35-fold in parameters.

versions.untested_parts: No held-out language-model cross-entropy loss or power-law loss fits; the study uses fMRI downstream scores.
No small-run power-law extrapolation to much larger language-model runs.
No test of stable power-law parameter/token allocation for fixed-compute language-model pretraining. The fMRI study selects candidates within its observed grid using downstream performance.
Architecture family is held fixed; the study does not compare depth, width, or architecture details at fixed parameter count.
Although fMRI is another modality, the study does not test whether the same power-law form holds; its downstream response analyses are not power-law loss tests.
Tests fMRI frozen linear-probe downstream scores, not language-model downstream tasks or performance as a function of pretraining loss.

Compares fitted downstream-response formulations and discusses limits to extrapolation in this fMRI setting; it does not test language-model loss exponents or compare published language-model power-law fits.

rows.subject: NeuroJEPA ID-response fit
rows.size_stated: 42 complete training runs; 4,125 saved models; six data sizes; seven model sizes
rows.operation_detail: Compared fitted response formulations using run and grouped-holdout diagnostics.
rows.measure: Run RMSE; run regret; held-out data-scale RMSE; held-out model-size RMSE; tail RMSE
rows.note: The paper says the fit compares candidates inside or close to the observed range, not far beyond it.
rows.check: Relinked from V7. The effective-data power-law response fits fMRI downstream ID error within the grid, including held-out data scale, held-out model size and tail splits (RMSE about 0.013). Measure is downstream error, not pretraining loss.

rows.subject: NeuroJEPA ID-response fit
rows.size_stated: 42 complete training runs; 4,125 saved models; six data sizes; seven model sizes
rows.operation_detail: Compared a response with no repeated-data decay.
rows.measure: Run RMSE; run regret; held-out data-scale RMSE; held-out model-size RMSE; tail RMSE
rows.note: The paper reports this formulation has higher run RMSE and regret than the response with data and capacity decay.
rows.check: Comparator, relinked from V7. Without repeated-data decay the power-law fit degrades (RMSE 0.0195 versus 0.0130).

rows.subject: NeuroJEPA ID-response fit
rows.size_stated: 42 complete training runs; 4,125 saved models; six data sizes; seven model sizes
rows.operation_detail: Compared repeated-data response correction with a model treating each repeated pass as new data.
rows.measure: Relative RMSE reduction; grouped-fold improvement
rows.baseline: model treating every repeated pass as new data
rows.value: RMSE reduced by 33.4%; improvement on all six grouped folds
rows.note: Most improvement is attributed to modeling diminishing value of repeated data passes.
rows.check: Relinked from V7. The repeated-data power-law form (Muennighoff Eq. 14) cuts holdout RMSE by 33.4% and improves all six folds.

rows.subject: NeuroJEPA ID-response fit
rows.size_stated: 42 complete training runs; 4,125 saved models; six data sizes; seven model sizes
rows.operation_detail: Assessed the incremental effect of adding the capacity-decay term to the data-only response.

conditions.value: data-only versus data plus capacity decay

rows.measure: RMSE change
rows.value: Adding the capacity-decay term changes RMSE by only 2.9%.
rows.note: The paper says the observed model range does not identify a finite capacity-decay scale.
rows.check: Relinked from V7. The capacity term adds only 2.9%, so the model-size side of the form is weakly identified.

rows.subject: NeuroJEPA ID-response fit
rows.size_stated: 42 complete training runs; 4,125 saved models; six data sizes; seven model sizes
rows.operation_detail: Bootstrapped the capacity-decay parameter estimate.
rows.measure: Fraction of bootstrap samples placing R*N at upper search bound
rows.note: Authors interpret this as failure of the current model range to identify a finite capacity-decay scale.
rows.check: Relinked from V7. R*N sits at its upper bound in 73% of bootstrap samples, so the capacity-decay scale is not identified in this range.

relationships.condition: fMRI NeuroJEPA models (2.65M–92.59M), frozen linear probes on 12 tasks
relationships.reason: Downstream error generally falls with compute, but not monotonically. Configurations at similar compute stay separated or swap order, so compute alone does not predict downstream performance (R1, R2).
relationships.display_finding: Downstream errors generally decreased with compute but sometimes reversed direction, while configurations at similar budgets remained separated or exchanged rankings.

relationships.condition: fMRI downstream ID error, within the observed data/model grid, with repeated data
relationships.reason: A Muennighoff-style power-law response with repeated-data decay fits held-out runs, data scales, model sizes and tails (RMSE about 0.013). Modelling repeat decay cuts RMSE by 33.4% (R24, R25, R27, R28).
relationships.display_finding: A power-law response incorporating repetition decay fits held-out errors with RMSE about 0.013, reducing RMSE by 33.4%.

relationships.condition: Model-size (capacity) side of the fMRI response

relationships.display_finding: Adding capacity decay improved the fit by only 2.9%, and its scale reached the search bound in 73% of bootstraps, leaving model-size dependence unidentified.
